notable_claims: Canadian universities (Manitoba, UBC) banned newsgroups or restricted equipment use to prevent access to pornographic material.
Wilfrid Laurier University used programs to scan for and delete 'nasty' filenames in the mid-eighties.
System administrators debated whether restricting public display of content constitutes censorship if private files remain accessible.
CPSR identified three privacy threats with NREN: commercial data selling, disclosure of network data, and government demands for electronic records.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes discussions on the censorship of newsgroups at Canadian universities, specifically regarding pornography and 'nasty' filenames. It includes perspectives from system administrators on balancing community responsibility with academic freedom and privacy concerns regarding the transition from NSFNet to NREN.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.43

notable_claims: The University of Manitoba banned all newsgroups dealing with sex following unfavorable publicity.
Blocking entire newsgroups rather than specific illegal content is characterized as censorship against academic tradition.
classification.summary: Dronon Brassmane shares a letter to the editor from The Globe & Mail criticizing the University of Manitoba's ban on sex-related newsgroups. The letter argues that banning entire categories of discussion is a 'heavy-handed' form of censorship that violates academic traditions of intellectual freedom. It suggests that universities should treat electronic media like libraries, ensuring access to all legally obtainable materials.
classification.title: Article 1--Censorship Update

notable_claims: The suppression of explicit sexual materials is relatively recent, roughly a hundred years old.
The Hicklin Rule allowed for the banning of works based on isolated passages and their effect on the most susceptible minds.
The Miller test requires that obscene material lack serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
Canadian obscenity law was influenced by MacKinnon and Dworkin's arguments regarding violence and degradation.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a historical overview of obscenity laws in the US, UK, and Canada to argue against censorship based on social mores. He discusses the evolution of legal tests for obscenity, from the Hicklin Rule to the Miller test, and mentions the influence of feminist legal theory on Canadian law. The post concludes by noting that despite claims that adult erotica is permitted, certain online spaces like alt.sex have been banned.
classification.title: Article 2--Re: "Computers graphic when it comes to porn"

notable_claims: Several cited studies challenge the Meese Commission's claim of a causal association between pornography and sexual violence.
Some research suggests that nonviolent erotica does not reliably predict negative attitudes toward women.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie of the EFF reposts a collection of academic abstracts from 1987-1989 regarding the effects of pornography on behavior and attitudes. The curated list specifically aims to provide scientific counterpoints to the conclusions of the 1986 Meese Commission. The studies examine correlations between sexually explicit materials, sexual offenses, and attitudes toward women.

identity.subject: Article 3--Re: "Computers graphic when it comes to porn"

notable_claims: University administrators may suppress material to avoid bad publicity rather than due to rational legal fear.
The right to possess obscene materials in private does not necessarily extend to a constitutional right to access 'obscene' Usenet News on school terminals.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legal risks of hosting obscene material on university networks. The author provides a historical survey of U.S. obscenity law and court cases to argue that while textual obscenity is rare, administrators often prioritize avoiding bad publicity over protecting academic freedom.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: "Computers graphic when it comes to porn"

identity.subject: Article 4--Re: "Computers graphic when it comes to porn"

notable_claims: The presence of graphic pornography in public university labs can create an exclusionary social environment for women.
There is a distinction between censoring discussion groups and removing explicit pictorial files (.gif) from public-facing monitors.
Institutional resource allocation should be weighed against the impact of hosting material that makes students uncomfortable.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the presence of sexually explicit material on Simon Fraser University's (SFU) altnet system. The author argues that while freedom of speech is important, institutions should consider the impact of graphic imagery in public computer labs and its role in reproducing patriarchal power dynamics. The post distinguishes between the censorship of discourse groups and the removal of unencoded graphic files.

notable_claims: System administrators have privileged access that bypasses standard user file protections
Automated keyword scanning could be used for sexual or political censorship
Export restrictions on DES software hindered the ability of non-US users to encrypt data for privacy
classification.summary: A. Daviel expresses concern over a directive from the University of British Columbia President to ensure university computing equipment is not used for pornographic material. The author argues that such directives encourage system administrators to use privileged access to scan users' private files and emails. This highlights the tension between institutional policy enforcement and the expectation of digital privacy in academic environments.
classification.title: Searching for computer porn at UBC

identity.subject: Article 6--Searching for computer porn at UBC

notable_claims: Publicly visible X-terminal screens and finger info are held to a 'PG-13' offensiveness standard.
Requiring content to be moved from a public display to a pointer/file is not considered censorship by the administrator.
Exposure to unsolicited obscene material in the workplace is categorized as harassment.
classification.summary: Elizabeth Schwartz, a system administrator at UMass Boston, defends the policy of limiting 'obscene' or offensive content in unsolicited public areas like finger (.plan) files and X-terminal screens. She argues that requiring users to place controversial material in separate publicly readable files rather than public displays is not censorship, but a measure against workplace harassment. The discussion centers on the distinction between banning content from a system and controlling its visibility in shared spaces.

notable_claims: Monitoring newsgroups to filter illegal material is impractical due to the volume and distribution of copyrighted content.
The 'common-carrier' argument is a potential legal defense for network providers against liability for user-posted content.
Illegal materials on networks are used as justification by authorities to implement broad censorship or discontinue access to the Altnet.
classification.summary: Jurgen Botz discusses the dilemma of hosting copyrighted and illegal materials on Usenet servers at an academic institution. He concludes that he will continue to carry all traffic to avoid acting as a censor and to preserve a 'common-carrier' legal defense. He expresses concern that the presence of illegal material provides ammunition for those seeking broad censorship of network access.
classification.title: Article 8--Follow-up: illegal material in newsgroups

notable_claims: Computing Services used a program to search for specific profane words in filenames.
A student's password containing a profane word was allegedly changed by administration.
Administrators justified the scanning based on complaints about profanity appearing on shared printer output and terminals.
classification.summary: A student newspaper article reports that Wilfrid Laurier University's Computing Services used a program to scan for profane words in filenames. While administrators claimed the tool was an obsolete 'hangover,' evidence suggested it had run recently and may have been used to force password changes. The incident sparked a debate over administrative surveillance of user data and the definition of acceptable language on academic systems.
classification.title: WLU sys admins search out "nasty" filenames and passwords

notable_claims: The NSF proposed splitting the backbone into a vBNS for research/education and NAPs for general traffic.
The vBNS was to be restricted to research and education traffic only.
Critics argued that the new architecture could disrupt regional cost-sharing arrangements that fostered widespread institutional connectivity.
classification.summary: Andrew Blau reports on a Communications Policy Forum meeting regarding the National Science Foundation's (NSF) plan to restructure the NSFNet backbone. The proposed architecture aimed to split services into a high-speed research backbone (vBNS) and commercial Network Access Points (NAPs). The EFF raised concerns about transparency in bidding, pricing for access, and the potential disruption of regional cost-sharing arrangements for academic institutions.
classification.title: The Future of NSFNet

notable_claims: Commercialization of NREN will create new pressures on privacy through the sale of user lists and transaction records.
Technical safeguards like cryptography are necessary but insufficient without legislative and legal protections.
The lack of a coherent federal privacy policy in the US hinders social acceptance of new digital networks.
organizations: National Commission on Libraries and Information Science (NCLIS)
classification.summary: Marc Rotenberg of CPSR testified before the National Commission on Libraries and Information Science regarding privacy protections for the National Research and Education Network (NREN). He argued that the commercialization of NREN would increase risks of data harvesting and government surveillance. The testimony emphasizes that while cryptography is useful, legal and policy frameworks are essential to protect intellectual freedom.
